None of the other selected Trigger, Memory, Threat, or Appraisal items indicate traumatic loss, so this strategy appears to target a different problem domain than the rest of the profile.

vignette: Camila was nine when the walls of her childhood home stopped feeling like boundaries and became stages. She remembers the heavy thud of a bookshelf toppling, the sharp crack of a ceramic mug shattering against the floorboards, and the sudden, frantic collision of two figures in the kitchen. For years, she told herself she only watched from the doorway, her chest pressed against the paint, certain that if she stayed perfectly still, the chaos would burn itself out. The memory does not arrive like a story; it arrives as a physical weight. When she closes her eyes, she can still taste the dust in the air and smell the sour, yeasty odor that clung to the perpetrator's shirt-a scent so vivid it sometimes pulls her out of the present before she can force it back. She knows she stops thinking about it the moment the images threaten to clarify, pushing the memory away before she can fully recall it. As Camila grew, her apartment's quiet no longer felt safe. She noticed her temper flare when a colleague's voice rose, snapping back sharply and leaving her convinced she had lost control. She began scanning every room upon entering, her eyes tracking hands and doorways, certain that bad things happened without warning and that she had no power to stop them. When news stories mentioned legal cases, a cold certainty settled in her stomach: those who caused harm never faced consequences, making waiting for justice a trick she refused to fall for. She stopped making any plans beyond the next few days. Scheduling a dinner in three weeks felt like signing a contract with an unsafe future. Her eating patterns tightened into a rigid routine; she measured portions strictly, not for health, but because controlling what went into her mouth was one of the few things that did not change without permission. At her job as an animator, the work usually offered a refuge, until it did not. Camila spent her days hunched over a graphics tablet, rendering character movements, but the studio had become a minefield. When a production assistant accidentally knocked a stack of sketchbooks off a nearby table, the sudden crash made her jolt so violently she had to grip her desk until her knuckles blanched. She told herself she could still work, but her hands would not steady. She avoided reference photos with crowded rooms or aggressive poses, deleting them before notice. Her avoidance of things that reminded her of the person who harmed her had quietly expanded into a broader withdrawal. She stopped responding to friend group messages, declined every invitation that required her to commit to a date, and told clients her rendering pipeline was under review when she actually just needed to disappear. The breaking point came when a corrupted file made her slam her palm against her desk, followed by a wave of nausea so intense she had to leave her workstation. She had come to believe she could not manage even the slightest upset without fracturing, and the exhaustion of constantly bracing for the next disruption had finally outpaced her will to hide it. Camila walked into the intake office with her bag clutched tightly in her lap, her shoulders still pulled forward as if expecting a blow. She was terrified that sitting through sessions would pull those childhood moments back into focus, that the smells and sounds would return and drown her out again. At the same time, she was hoping, quietly and almost secretly, that someone might help her untangle the rules she had built to survive the past from the life she was trying to live now.
